title: Lusheng
summary: The lusheng is a mouth organ of the Miao and Dong peoples of south-west China: six bamboo pipes of different lengths rise from a wooden wind chest, each with a small reed inside. Players blow into the chest and cover a hole on a pipe to sound it, often swaying or stepping together in a circle.
howToPlay: Six upright pipes stand on a wooden wind chest; a mark travels toward the pipe you must sound.
Press the pipe's hole as its mark reaches the line and hold the longer notes.
Keep to the stepping beat: the closer to the beat, the higher the score.
rules: Six pipes give six notes of a five-note scale; the longer the pipe, the lower the note.
Two figures are played once each: a rising and falling line, and a swaying stepping figure in four beats to the bar.
A note on the beat scores in full, a close one scores less, and an extra stroke costs a little.
Three stars need 90 percent, two 70 percent, one 40 percent.
heritageNote: The lusheng is played by the Miao (Hmong), Dong and neighbouring peoples in Guizhou, Guangxi and Yunnan, and in parts of Laos and Vietnam. Groups of players sway and step in circles at village gatherings and festivals, and the pipes range from a hand-held size to ones taller than a person.
